Supreme Court’s Dred Scott v. Sandford decision (1857), which had held that Black people (free or enslaved) were not and could never be U.S. citizens, and to secure citizenship for formerly enslaved people and their descendants after the Civil War. It also constitutionalized (and broadened) the Civil Rights Act of 1866, which declared that “all persons born in the United States and not subject to any foreign power, excluding Indians not taxed, are hereby declared to be citizens.”

Key Elements of Original Intent from Congressional Debates

•  Codification of jus soli (citizenship by birthplace): This drew from English common law and pre-existing American practice for free white persons born in the country. The framers aimed to make it explicit, race-neutral, and constitutionally protected against future political reversal. brennancenter.org 
•  The qualifier “subject to the jurisdiction thereof”: This was not meant to create broad exclusions based on parental immigration status or race. It primarily excluded:
•  Children of foreign diplomats (who enjoyed immunity and owed allegiance elsewhere).
•  Members of Indian tribes living under tribal authority (not fully subject to U.S. laws, as tribes were treated as separate sovereigns; this was later addressed by statute and the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924). constitutioncenter.org 
Senator Jacob Howard (R-MI), who introduced the clause in the Senate on May 30, 1866, explained: “This amendment which I have offered is simply declaratory of what I regard as the law of the land already, that every person born within the limits of the United States, and subject to their jurisdiction, is by virtue of natural law and national law a citizen of the United States.
